query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Minor yttrium doping (0.5–2 at.%) in high-entropy boride components (e.g., (TiZrHfTaNb)B2) will promote the in-situ formation of a continuous, adherent yttrium-aluminate (Y–Al–O) surface scale upon exposure to molten aluminum. This protective scale will act as an effective diffusion barrier, significantly reducing the molten aluminum corrosion rate compared to undoped components.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy boride components (e.g., (TiZrHfTaNb)B2) synthesized without yttrium doping via reactive spark plasma sintering, exhibiting a primarily homogeneous phase.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor doping of yttrium (0.5–2 at.%) into the boride during synthesis to ensure a uniform distribution within the material.
generation.conditions: The engineered components will be exposed to hot-dip aluminum plating conditions, specifically molten aluminum environments at ~700–750 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The doping induces yttrium segregation during high-temperature exposure, leading to the formation of a continuous yttrium-aluminate (Y–Al–O) layer at the component surface.
generation.mechanism: During exposure to molten aluminum, yttrium reacts with trace oxygen (or residual aluminum oxide) to form a thermodynamically stable, adherent Y–Al–O scale. This protective scale serves as a diffusion barrier that impedes further penetration of molten aluminum, thereby reducing corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Yttrium-doped components will show significantly lower corrosion rates, improved surface stability (as evidenced by reduced weight loss, shallower corrosion depths, and intact oxide scales), and enhanced overall durability compared to undoped counterparts.
generation.baseline: Undoped high-entropy boride components (e.g., (TiZrHfTaNb)B2) processed under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected under standard hot-dip aluminum plating parameters (~700–750 °C), with the optimal yttrium content maintained within the 0.5–2 at.% range. Deviations from this range or significantly different environmental oxygen levels might reduce the effectiveness of the protective scale formation.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism is supported by established reactive element effects in high-temperature oxides, the precise quantitative improvement in corrosion resistance remains uncertain until validated by controlled experimental studies under relevant operating conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy boride samples: one set doped with 0.5–2 at.% yttrium and one undoped (control). Both sample sets will be fabricated using the same synthesis methods (e.g., spark plasma sintering) and then exposed to molten aluminum under hot-dip plating conditions (700–750 °C) for a fixed period.
measurements: Weight loss measurements after exposure to assess overall corrosion extent.
Cross-sectional microscopic analysis (SEM/EDS) to measure corrosion depth and oxide scale integrity.
In-situ oxidation kinetics via thermogravimetric analysis to compare the oxidation behavior.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yttrium-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., a measurable reduction in corrosion rate, weight loss, or corrosion depth beyond experimental uncertainty) compared to the undoped samples, the hypothesis will be falsified.

This manuscript shows the study of the structure, mechanical, and chemical properties of high-entropy borides MeB2 (Me = Ti, Ta, Nb, Hf, Zr). High-entropy borides were synthesized by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering. A chemically homogeneous powder with a low iron content (0.12%) was obtained in a planetary mill by rotating the planetary disk/pots at 200–400 rpm and a processing time of 7.5 h. The structure, mechanical, and chemical properties of the resulting high-entropy borides have been studied. A single-phase hexagonal structure is formed during spark plasma sintering of mechanically alloyed powders at 2000 °C. The microhardness of the samples ranged from 1763 to 1959 HV. Gas-dynamic tests of the synthesized materials showed that an increase in the content of Zr and Hf in the composition increases the thermal-oxidative resistance of the material.

At temperatures exceeding 500 °C, the oxidation behavior of traditional and complex alloys (e.g., Ni-Cr, Ni-based superalloys, Fe-Cr, CoCrFeNiMn ‘Cantor’ alloy) has been extensively studied in oxygen-rich environments and over extended periods (from days to hundreds of days,). Key contributors to the process include species transport to the oxide/metal junction within the base alloy, movement across the oxide/metal interface, and passage through the oxide layer. For instance, atmospheric oxidation of CoCrFeNiMn-containing alloys results in a layered oxide film, with Cr-rich inner and Mn-rich outer oxides attributed to outward cation diffusion. In a study by Kim et al., the high-temperature oxidation of FeCrMnNiCo (900–1100 °C in 20% O2/80% N2 for 24 h) showed the formation of layered Cr2O3 and Mn2O3 oxides at 900 °C. This process led to Ni, Fe, and Co enrichment in the base alloy. At 1000–1100 °C, the outer Mn2O3 layer changed to Mn3O4, forming a (Mn, Cr)3O4 ternary oxide with Ni, Fe, and Co in a solid solution. In addition, to obtain a uniform and stable protective layer, sputtering technology offers a fast deposition rate and a low-cost solution. Although the development of HEA systems has been going on for more than a decade, there are few reports on the deposition of stable protective films on HEA surfaces by conventional reactive sputtering techniques. Many studies have shown that sputter deposition of CrN film on conventional stainless steel is beneficial for its wear and corrosion resistance [,]. The CrN film deposited on the surface of 316 stainless steel has a positive effect on the friction behavior in NaCl solution and high temperature environments until heated to 550 °C []. In the tribo-corrosion test, the CrN coating layer can also remain relatively stable during the ball-on-plate sliding under various applied potentials []. As stainless steels are similar to CoCrNi-based MEAs in terms of their single FCC structure and lattice constant, this study attempts to sputter CrN film with a Cr buffer layer on the surface of CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA and discusses in detail the improvement of corrosion and wear resistance of CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA by sputtering CrN film.

proposals.intervention: Introduce a minor doping of yttrium (0.5–2 at.%) into the boride composition during synthesis
proposals.conditions: Components operate under hot-dip aluminum plating conditions (~700–750 °C) in direct contact with molten aluminum
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation of a thermally stable, continuous yttrium-aluminate (Y–Al–O) surface layer
proposals.mechanism: Yttrium segregates to the surface during high-temperature exposure and reacts with trace oxygen (or residual Al-oxide) to form an adherent, protective Y–Al–O scale. This barrier reduces molten aluminum penetration and slows down corrosive attack
proposals.predicted_outcome: Doped components achieve a significantly reduced corrosion rate and less oxide scale spallation relative to undoped boride materials, as measured by weight loss and microscopic examination of corrosion depth
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By altering the surface chemistry through Y-doping, the proposed intervention creates an in-situ barrier layer that directly impedes molten aluminum corrosion without altering the bulk boride composition

proposals.intervention: Apply a surface mechanical attrition treatment (SMAT) to generate an ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer
proposals.conditions: Surface treatment performed at room temperature followed by exposure to molten aluminum environments at plating operating temperatures (~700–750 °C)
proposals.structural_mediator: Creation of a nanocrystalline near-surface layer with high density of grain boundaries
proposals.mechanism: The refined, nanostructured layer promotes rapid and uniform oxidation to form a coherent protective oxide. The high density of grain boundaries acts as both a fast diffusion pathway for beneficial oxides and a barrier to penetration by molten aluminum
proposals.predicted_outcome: SMAT-treated components would exhibit lower corrosion rates and enhanced surface stability under molten-aluminum exposure relative to untreated boride surfaces, measurable via in-situ oxidation kinetics and corrosion depth analysis
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This intervention uses processing-induced microstructural modification to create a robust, passivating oxide network, effectively resisting molten aluminum attack with a single surface treatment step

proposals.material_system: Boride-based composite, such as TiB2 reinforced with ZrC
proposals.intervention: Incorporate a fine dispersion of ZrC particles into the boride matrix via a modified powder metallurgy process
proposals.conditions: Synthesis by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering under temperatures similar to those used for high-entropy borides (near 2000 °C), ensuring uniform dispersion; operation in molten aluminum (~700–750 °C)
proposals.structural_mediator: A composite microstructure with ZrC second-phase particles homogeneously distributed in the boride matrix
proposals.mechanism: ZrC particles act as physical diffusion barriers that interrupt continuous pathways for molten aluminum attack. They also help to stabilize the overall microstructure at high temperatures, reducing the effective reactive surface area
proposals.predicted_outcome: The modified composite is expected to show a lower corrosion rate (quantified through weight loss or depth profiling) compared to the homogeneous boride baseline, with improved resistance to molten aluminum penetration
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By adding a secondary refractory phase, the intervention creates microstructural heterogeneities that disrupt corrosive flow paths, offering a single-process modification to improve molten-aluminum corrosion resistance

proposals.intervention: Implement an optimized heat-treatment protocol to induce a controlled dual-phase microstructure with intergranular intermetallic precipitates
proposals.conditions: Post-synthesis thermal treatment at ~2000 °C with controlled cooling rates under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation, followed by exposure to molten aluminum at plating temperatures (~700–750 °C)
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation of secondary intermetallic phases at grain boundaries within the primarily boride matrix
proposals.mechanism: The precipitated intermetallic phases preferentially locate at grain boundaries, acting as barriers that limit the diffusion and infiltration of molten aluminum by providing chemically inert interfaces
proposals.predicted_outcome: Heat-treated components are expected to show considerably lower molten-aluminum corrosion (assessed by corrosion rate tests and interfacial analysis) compared to as-sintered, single-phase boride materials
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This thermally driven microstructural tuning method targets the inherent corrosion pathways by reinforcing grain boundaries, thereby directly addressing the vulnerability of boride components to molten aluminum attack in a single intervention step

decision.rationale: Direction B was chosen because doping the boride with a minor amount of yttrium directly targets the molten aluminum corrosion issue by promoting the in-situ formation of a continuous, thermodynamically stable yttrium-aluminate (Y–Al–O) protective scale. This mechanism leverages the well-known reactive element effect, which helps improve oxide adherence and barrier properties, thereby reducing corrosion rates. Although other directions (such as SMAT or composite reinforcement) offer potential benefits, the chemical modification via Y-doping is more robust at the operational temperatures (~700–750 °C) of hot-dip aluminum plating, and it requires only a single intervention during synthesis. The supporting evidence from past studies on oxide formation and corrosion resistance in high-temperature environments (as reflected in the allowed evidence records) provides a basis for this hypothesis, even though exact quantitative improvements remain to be established experimentally.
